title: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings
hook: jeea jant ke thaakuraa: Lord of all beings, pervading all (Sukhmani 22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 21, and your line: behind all things. Did you catch a little quiet before the day's noise? The twenty-first ashtpadi brought the world into being. The twenty-second looks at who lives in it. Day five hundred twenty-two.

A single ant on the kitchen counter, walking a careful line toward a grain of sugar. Most of us have a reflex for that moment: a paper towel, a thumb. But if you stop and actually watch it, it's remarkable. It's carrying something heavier than itself. It's checking the way with its antennae. It's going somewhere, for some reason that matters to it. The twenty-second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming the Lord of that ant, and of everything else that breathes.
screen: `ONE ANT ON THE COUNTER.` → `IT'S GOING SOMEWHERE.` → `THE LORD OF EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: Lord and Master of all beings and creatures, You Yourself are present in all of them. Nanak says: the One is spread out everywhere; where could a second be seen? Start with jeea jant. Jeea are living beings, things with life and breath. Jant are creatures, every kind of animal. Together the phrase is Gurbani's way of saying everyone and everything alive: people, ants, birds, fish, the cat on the windowsill. Thaakur is lord or master, a word of respect for the one in charge of a household or estate. So the salok begins: Master of every living thing. But the second half changes what master means. God isn't pictured as a landlord far off, collecting rent. Aape vartanhaar: God Himself is the one moving within them all, present and active in each. And then the last line: eko pasariaa. The One has spread out. Where is there a second to see? This is why Sikh teaching speaks so warmly about all living things. If the same One is spread through every creature, then the ant on the counter isn't simply a pest or a stranger. It's kin, in a real sense: made by the same Master, filled by the same presence. That doesn't mean Sikhs never swat a mosquito. It means the glance you give a living thing can carry a little respect. Today's ashtpadi begins by widening the circle of who counts.
screen: `JEEA JANT: EVERYTHING ALIVE.` · `THAAKUR: LORD AND MASTER.` · `NOT FAR OFF: MOVING WITHIN.` · `EKO PASARIAA: THE ONE, SPREAD OUT.` · then, large: `LORD OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel kin to a creature. Find a living thing you can see or hear: a bird outside, a houseplant, a pet, a fly on the window, even a picture of an animal you love. Watch it for a while. Notice its breathing, its movement, the way it pays attention to its world. Then quietly hold the thought: the same Master, the same life. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru as you watch. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 22. Its salok calls God thaakur of jeea jant, Master of every living thing, and says the One is spread through them all.
Your line: lord of all. Today, when you meet an insect indoors, try carrying it outside instead. Day five hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi begin with a salok naming God the Master of all living beings, the One spread through every creature.

myth: the salok pictures God as a distant landlord
aape vartanhaar: God is the one moving within all beings.
jeea jant means every living thing, people and animals
Gurbani's way of saying everything alive.
the salok says there is a second power beside the One
it asks: the One is spread everywhere; where could a second be seen?

fork.setup: an ant crosses your counter. by the twenty-second salok, what is it?
options: a creature whose Master is the same One, spread through all.
fork.reveal: the salok calls God the thaakur of jeea jant, Master of every living being, present within each one.

original.note: Gurmukhi: thaakur, lord or master; in the salok, thaakuraa, Lord of all beings.

trapdoor: what you thought: lord of all means God is the boss of everything.
what it means: the Master of every living being is also present within each one, so all life is kin.
what a scholar hears: eko pasariaa, the One spread out, answers its own question: where could a second be seen? No second power appears anywhere.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 22, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 291)

notes: Paraphrase of the ashtpadi 22 salok (jeea jant ke thaakuraa aape vartanhaar; naanak eko pasariaa doojaa kah drisataar): confirm and confirm Ang.
The line about swatting a mosquito is a light, non-doctrinal aside; a Keeper may prefer to cut it.
